status.text:
WTF is PHP and why is the Prime Minister of Japan telling companies to take their websites offline if they can't update in time? And why did a company whose whole job is proving websites are legit use the number 4 as its secret key?

If you are non-technical, I wrote this for you. Some massive compromises and vulnerabilities came to light in the last 72 hours. Here's a list of the affected tools and how bad each one is:

PHP: programming language used by ~70% of all websites.
Two flaws nicknamed "PHP2Shell" let anyone on the internet, without logging in, send a website a specially crafted request that scrambles its memory and lets them run their own commands on the server. That effectively means taking over the website. Details leaked a day early, and criminals started attacking sites before the fix was even out. Fixed, but sites need to update now.
https://www.php.net/archive/2026.php#2026-10-21-5

GitLab: workspace where teams build, test, and manage their app code, with 50M+ users and about half of the 100 largest US companies as customers.
Rated 10 out of 10, the maximum severity. Attackers could run their own commands on GitLab servers without logging in and without anyone clicking anything, and it affects every version going back 12 years. That could expose a company's private code and the passwords and keys stored alongside it. Fixed, but servers need to update.
https://docs.gitlab.com/releases/patches/patch-release-gitlab-19-5-1-released/

Adobe Commerce / Magento: software behind ~110000 online stores, including about 1 in 5 of the 1000 biggest US online retailers.
CVE-2026-103849 is rated 10 out of 10, the maximum severity. Anyone on the internet, without logging in, could take complete control of an online store, including its customer data, orders, and potentially its payment pages. Adobe released a fix on Oct 13, but working attack code went public on Oct 18 and researchers expect attacks on stores that haven't updated to start any day.
https://www.adobe.com/trust/security/products/commerce/apsb26-153

PingCAP / TiDB Cloud: cloud service that companies like banks, game studios and online shops use to run their databases.
Hackers got into PingCAP's internal systems for nearly a month using stolen logins and copied customer account info, billing records, and source code. PingCAP confirmed that much, but says customers' actual stored data wasn't touched. The hackers claim far worse: 10.6 TB stolen, logins sitting in PingCAP's own code, and staff pasting customer passwords into support tickets. They've released 200 GB as proof, but those claims aren't verified yet.
https://runtimewire.com/article/pingcap-tidb-cloud-data-exposure-stolen-credentials

Plex Media Server: one of the most popular and widely deployed consumer home media server platforms available.
Four flaws chained together, nicknamed "Plex2Shell," let anyone on the internet take over the computer running Plex without a password. Criminals are already using it in real attacks, and the US cybersecurity agency (CISA) has put it on its official list of actively exploited flaws.
https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2026/10/20/cisa-adds-six-known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog

eMudhra: India's largest issuer of digital ID certificates (50M+ issued), including the ones websites use to prove they're legit.
Its master signing keys are supposed to be random numbers over 100 digits long. Eight were under 256, and one was literally the number 4. Anyone holding them could forge website IDs that browsers trust, letting a criminal pose as your bank with no warning. Browsers blocked them within hours, but un-updated devices may still trust them. This also caused the Java issue below.
https://emudhra.com/en/post/certificate-security-incident

LiteLLM: translator tool that connects apps to different AI services, downloaded ~90 million times a month.
Attackers published a booby-trapped version (1.107.0) on the official download sites. Anyone who installed it got malware that steals passwords and keys and lets the attacker run commands on their machine every hour. It was online for about 2 hours before being pulled. Version 1.106.2 is the last safe one.
https://docs.litellm.ai/blog/security-incident-oct-21-2026

Node.js: programming language that runs the servers behind about a quarter of the world's 1000 biggest websites.
An attacker could send an app booby-trapped data that corrupts its memory and lets them run their own commands on its server, effectively taking it over. Fixed, but apps need to update.
https://nodejs.org/en/blog/vulnerability/october-2026-security-releases

Railway: cloud platform with 2M+ users for launching websites and managing app databases.
Intruders broke into the system where customers store their apps' secret passwords and keys, and some of those secrets were readable. That includes keys to paid services and passwords to databases. Every customer should change all of them.
https://blog.railway.com/p/security-disclosure-wednesday-october-21st

Java: programming language that runs core systems at half of the 100 largest US companies.
Because of the weak eMudhra keys, Java's secure-connection system could be tricked into trusting fake websites. An attacker on the internet, without logging in, could read or tamper with data that was supposed to be private. Fixed, but systems need to update.
https://www.oracle.com/security-alerts/alert-cve-2026-91403.html

OVHcloud CLI: tool for controlling servers on OVHcloud, Europe's largest cloud provider (1.6M customers).
Someone hijacked the developer's GitHub account and swapped the downloadable program (versions 0.11.0–0.15.0) for malware that steals passwords and keys. Anyone who downloaded it during that 94-minute window should assume their secrets were stolen. The original code itself was not touched.
https://github.com/ovh/ovhcloud-cli/security/advisories/GHSA-862f-55f5-vmvw

To the best of my knowledge, fixes are out for all the ones that need them, but they only help once installed.
